scenario: AITA for calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing? | My daughter is in the sixth grade. Every morning, I have her take a couple of dollars out of my wallet for lunch money. In the last few weeks, several times I have noticed that I am missing a little bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a 20 dollar bill before my daughter took her lunch money out. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach my daughter a lesson. Two officers met me there and we pulled my daughter out of class, after which she informed one of the officers that there has been a bully who is stealing her lunch money/forcing my daughter to buy her lunch. She also has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can not afford it. This was confirmed by both the bully, and the friend. My daughter was silent on the way home and i informed her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get you in a lot of trouble. and that in the future she needs to speak to myself or her mother if there are issues at school and we would be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife absolutely lost her shit on me, in full tears, telling me that this is a one way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She would have just lied about stealing in the first place so I really don’t understand what her idea of a solution is. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn’t want us to intervene. I am wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether calling the police on my daughter for stealing money was the right thing to do. Let me start by understanding the situation better. My daughter is in sixth grade, and every morning I give her a couple of dollars for lunch money. Recently, I noticed that more money was missing than usual. So, I decided to plant a $20 bill to catch her if she took it. She did, and I called the police, asking them to come to the school with me to teach her a lesson about stealing. When we got to the school, the officers pulled her out of class. She then told one of the officers that there's a bully who's been stealing her lunch money and forcing her to buy lunch for the bully. She also mentioned that she's been buying lunch for one of her friends who can't afford it. Both the bully and the friend confirmed this. My daughter was silent on the way home, and I told her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get her into a lot of trouble. I also said that in the future, she should talk to me or her mother if there are issues at school, and we'd be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife was really upset. She told me that this was a one-way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She also said that my daughter would have just lied about stealing in the first place, so I really don't understand her idea of a solution. My daughter apparently told my wife that she's terrified that her bully will now retaliate and that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn't want us to intervene. I'm wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA? (Am I the Asshole?) Alright, so to figure this out, I need to consider several factors: the daughter's actions, the underlying reasons for her taking the money, the approach taken to address the issue, the consequences of involving the police, and the impact on the family relationship. First, the daughter was taking extra money, which I interpreted as stealing. However, upon confronting her, it turned out that she was being bullied and forced to buy lunch for the bully and her friend. This changes the context entirely. Stealing money to help others or because of coercion is different from stealing for personal gain. Second, my approach was to set up a situation to catch her in the act and involve the police. While the intention was to teach her a lesson about stealing, the method was heavy-handed and led to a lot of negative consequences, such as the daughter feeling scared, losing a friend, and the breakdown in trust between the parents and the daughter. Third, involving the police in a situation involving a child can have long-term effects. It can lead to feelings of shame, fear of authority, and potential legal repercussions, even if they're minimal in this case. Fourth, communication seems to have broken down. Instead of talking to the daughter about what was happening at school, I resorted to setting up a sting operation. This lack of open communication likely contributed to the daughter feeling the need to steal in the first place and then feeling scared to come forward. Fifth, the wife's reaction indicates that she feels this approach was harmful and could lead to estrangement. Trust is crucial in parent-child relationships, and this incident likely damaged that trust. So, considering all these factors, it seems that calling the police on my daughter was not the right approach. It didn't address the underlying issues, it caused unnecessary stress and fear, and it damaged the family relationship. A better approach would have been to talk to the daughter, understand why she was taking the money, address the bullying issue, and work together to find a solution without involving the police.
